The passage is in Aristotle, Historia animalium (History of Animals) IX.1. What Aristotle is doing Book IX is a collection of observations about animal behavior and interspecies relationships—friendship, hostility, cooperation, nesting, feeding, etc. Very early in IX.1, Aristotle gives a list of birds that are supposedly hostile to one another: ὁ ἄνθος καὶ ἡ ἀκανθὶς καὶ ὁ αἰγίθος ἀλλήλοις εἰσὶν ἐχθροί Something like: “The anthus, the acanthis, and the aegithus are enemies of one another.” The crucial word is ἀκανθίς (akanthís). The Perseus vocabulary database identifies the word in this exact passage as “the goldfinch.” Immediately afterward Aristotle says that the blood of the anthus will not mix with the blood of the aegithus, and then continues cataloguing supposed friendships and enmities among animals. Then, later in the same book, he returns to the acanthis: “The acanthis finds its food with difficulty; its plumage is poor, but its note is musical.” That's in IX.12/13 depending on edition/chapter division. So this is not a lexicon guessing that akanthis might be a bird. Aristotle himself uses ἀκανθίς as the name of an actual bird. And this gives us a potentially important distinction for your memory: ἄκανθος / ἄκανθα = acanthus / thorn Ἀκάνθιος = Acanthian, from Acanthus ἀκανθίς = a bird, conventionally identified as goldfinch/finch ἀκανθίδες = plural birds Those are very easy forms to conflate if one encountered them in a secondary source, manuscript, lexicon, or magical text. So this isn't just: “There is a word that happens to mean a bird.” It is: An actual magical papyrus contains an obscure AKANTH- word whose first editors thought meant a bird, while later editors decided it meant the acanthus plant. That's a very unusual textual instability. 2. And the bird reading isn't remotely implausible Because ἀκανθίς genuinely is a bird. The Cambridge Greek Lexicon gives: ἀκανθίς, -ίδος — “a songbird; perhaps finch” with Theocritus as a literary witness. The Greek-language LSJ digest is even more explicit: ἀκανθίς — είδος πτηνού, καρδελίνα “a kind of bird, goldfinch,” citing Aristotle and Theocritus. And Aristotle's History of Animals actually places it among birds that feed on thistles: ἀκανθοφάγα, ἀκανθίς, θραυπίς... “These and similar [birds] are thorn-eaters: the acanthis, the thraupis…” So an ancient reader encountering ἄκανθις could quite legitimately have understood: a bird associated with thorns. 3. There is an even better ancient association: ἀκανθίς + dove This keeps getting more interesting. Aristotle's bird discussion gives us the ἀκανθίς. But the classical poetic tradition also puts ἀκανθίδες and τρυγών together: ᾄδον κορυδοὶ καὶ ἀκανθίδες, ἔστενε τρυγών roughly: “Larks and acanthides sang; the turtle-dove mourned.” This is the Theocritean line behind the traditional identification of ἀκανθίς with the linnet/goldfinch. The later lexicographical tradition preserves exactly this example. So there really is an ancient textual neighborhood containing: ἀκανθίς — thorn-associated songbird τρυγών — turtle-dove Again, not “Acanthian dove.” But it makes your remembered compound considerably less alien to Greek literary vocabulary. 4. Now the magical doves The PGM corpus contains several genuine dove rituals. One especially useful example is PGM VIII 69–73, where a magical ink/mixture calls for: αἷμα περιστερᾶς λευκῆς “blood of a white dove.” The same formula survives in a parallel version in PGM VII, where the text has a notorious textual problem around μίλτον. The newer scholarship discusses whether Preisendanz was right to supplement the text with καὶ αἷμα (“and blood”). That's exactly the kind of thing you asked us to investigate: different editions can materially change what the magical text appears to say. And there are other dove rituals: white dove blood occurs in magical writing/ink; white dove material occurs in ritual preparations; PGM XIII includes a sacrificial sequence involving a περιστερά. So “dove” is unquestionably part of the magical papyrus vocabulary. 5. There's a potentially important third word: πελειά / πελειάς This may actually be more promising than περιστερά. Greek has several words for dove, but πέλεια / πελειάς is particularly interesting because of its religious and oracular associations. The Peleiai are the sacred doves associated with Dodona—and, by extension, the prophetic women/priestesses associated with the oracle. So if whatever you remember was not literally περιστερά, we could be looking for: ἀκανθ- + πελειά / πελειάς rather than: ἀκανθ- + περιστερά I have not found that combination in the magical papyri, but this is now one of the searches I'd prioritize. 6. Another thing I found that I think matters The PGM material isn't simply a collection of random spells. Some of it explicitly preserves secret equivalences. The PGM XII passage itself says that the practitioners had collected the solutions to the names of herbs and other things from many copies of these texts (ἀντιγράφων), and that these were secret. A modern study of the passage emphasizes that we're dealing with a tradition of encoded/decoded ingredient names. That matters enormously for your question. If you encountered a secondary source discussing the PGM tradition, it's entirely possible that what entered your memory wasn't the literal papyrus wording. It could have been an editorial interpretation, a gloss, a translation, or a reconstruction. In other words, “Acanthian Dove” might be a memory of something that never occurs verbatim in the surviving Greek, but that an editor or scholar described in those terms. 7. And there's a really weird mythological bridge Ἀκανθίς / Ἀκανθυλλίς is not only the name of a bird. In Antoninus Liberalis' Metamorphoses 7, Acanthis/Acanthyllis is a human girl who is transformed into a bird along with her family. The ancient mythographic tradition therefore literally has: Acanthis → bird and the name of the transformed woman is the same as the bird-name ἀκανθίς. That is an important distinction from “Acanthian” as a geographical adjective. The Acanth- bird tradition is therefore internally mythological, not merely zoological. 8. What I think may have happened to your memory At this point I see three increasingly plausible reconstructions. Hypothesis A — the word was Acanthis, not Acanthian This is now my favorite. You may have encountered: Ἀκανθίς / ἀκανθίς and subsequently remembered it in English as Acanthian. That would explain why the phrase feels like an old proper name rather than an ordinary adjective. And Acanthis is genuinely a bird-name in Greek. Hypothesis B — the memory fused two magical ingredients Something like: ἄκανθις + αἷμα περιστερᾶς λευκῆς could have become, in memory: Acanthian dove That sounds speculative—but we now know that both components genuinely occur in the magical corpus. Hypothesis C — there was an editorial/secondary-source formulation This is the one I most want to investigate next. The PGM XII ἄκανθις/ἄκανθος disagreement proves that modern editors are already doing exactly the kind of interpretive work that could generate an unusual English expression. If some older commentary described an ingredient as something like “the acanthine bird,” “acanthis,” “thorn-bird,” etc., and elsewhere discussed a dove, the compound could have entered your memory from a secondary scholarly source rather than an ancient text. One correction to our search strategy I don't think we should search only for the English phrase anymore. The high-value search set is now: Ἀκανθίς ἀκανθίς Ἀκανθυλλίς ἀκανθυλλίς Ἀκάνθιος ἀκάνθιος ἄκανθος ἄκανθα περιστερά πελειά / πελειάς τρυγών ἀκανθίς + ὄρνις ἀκανθίς + ἱερός ἀκανθίς + αἷμα ἀκανθίς + δῶρον ἀκανθίς + ἄγγελος / ἀγγέλλω ἀκανθίς + πέμπω and, crucially, not just PGM but PDM, GEMF, Greek magical formularies outside the PGM corpus, the Kyranides, Cyranides/physiological magic, magical handbooks, Christian magical papyri, and Byzantine magical/medical compilations. My assessment right now I would put the evidentiary status this way: “Acanthian Dove” as an attested ancient phrase: ❌ not found. Acanth-/acanthis + bird in ancient Greek: ✅ absolutely attested. Acanth-/acanthis in Greek magical papyri: ✅ absolutely attested, with a significant editorial dispute over whether it is a bird or plant. Dove in Greek magical papyri: ✅ extensively attested. Acanthis + dove in ancient Greek textual vicinity: ✅ yes, especially the Aristotelian/Theocritean bird vocabulary. A surviving ancient source that explains your exact phrase: still missing. And that last category is the one I think is worth pursuing rather than giving up. The PGM XII ἄκανθις problem is now the lead I would follow. The fact that a magical manuscript itself gives us an obscure akanth- term, while editors for more than a century have disagreed whether the word is a bird or a plant, is too close to your remembered object to leave unexplored. [QUERENT] [not in the paste] [ANSWER 6] Yes — Theophrastus is a very worthwhile place to check, and I think the result actually changes how I'd interpret the PGM XII evidence. Theophrastus does have the ἀκανθ- vocabulary In Historia plantarum 1.10, Theophrastus discusses different kinds of leaves, including ἀκανθόφυλλα (“thorn-/spine-leaved” plants) and ἄκανθα (“thorn/spine”). He is explicitly trying to establish botanical terminology and even argues that a thorn can function morphologically as a modified leaf. The particularly relevant passage is HP 1.10.6: ἀκανθῶδες δὲ ἐκ τῶν ἄκρων... “thorny/spiny at the extremities…” and then: φυλλάκανθον... “leaf-thorn…” followed by his discussion of plants such as ἄκανος and the general class of ἀκανώδη plants. So Theophrastus gives us an important piece of the lexical background: ἄκανθα / ἀκανθώδης / ἀκανθόφυλλα are firmly established botanical terminology well before the magical papyri. But here's the more interesting passage In HP 4.4, discussing plants encountered in Asia, Theophrastus repeatedly uses ἄκανθα. At 4.4.11, he says: Ἐν δὲ τῇ Ἀρίᾳ χώρᾳ ... ἄκανθά ἐστιν, ἐφ’ ἧς γίνεται δάκρυον ὅμοιον τῇ σμύρνῃ... “There is in the country called Aria a thorn, upon which there is produced a tear/resin resembling myrrh…” And at 4.4.13 he describes another extraordinary ἄκανθα that has no leaves, grows from a single root, has extremely sharp spines, and produces a juice when the spines are broken or rubbed. This is particularly relevant because PGM XII's disputed ἄκανθις is precisely the sort of word that could have been understood botanically in the Theophrastean tradition. But I don't find a dove in Theophrastus I specifically checked for: περιστερά — pigeon/dove τρυγών — turtle-dove πέλεια / πελειάς — dove ἀκανθίς combinations of the above and I am not finding a Theophrastean “Acanthian dove.” That's significant. The Historia plantarum is fundamentally a botanical work; its surviving Greek text is available in the Hort edition through Perseus, and the work is divided into nine surviving books. So Theophrastus gives us excellent evidence for the acanth- side, but not presently for the dove side. But there's a subtle thing here that I think matters Theophrastus' ἄκανθα isn't necessarily “the acanthus.” That's easy to miss. He uses ἄκανθα as a much broader botanical category for a thorn/spine-bearing plant. In 4.4 he applies it to exotic plants producing resins and poisonous juices. So when the PGM has: ἄκανθις and modern editors propose emending/interpreting it as ἄκανθος/ἄκανθα, they are operating inside an already very old Theophrastean botanical vocabulary. That makes the PGM XII controversy more interesting, not less. The really important question: does Theophrastus ever use ἀκανθίς? This is where I would not yet claim a negative. The ordinary searchable versions of Historia plantarum are imperfect, and “ἀκανθίς” is particularly vulnerable to OCR/search problems because it can occur in discussions of: ἄκανθα ἀκανθώδης ἀκανθόφυλλα ἀκανθίς as well as in apparatus/commentary rather than the running text. There are multiple editions to compare: Wimmer's critical edition, Hort's Loeb, and the older Aldine/early printed tradition. Perseus catalogs Hort's Greek edition, while the Wellcome copy gives us Wimmer's 1842 critical text. And this is exactly where I think we should go next. I want to check four layers separately: The Greek manuscripts/critical text of Theophrastus Wimmer's apparatus Hort's Greek text + translation/notes Ancient botanical commentators and later lexica citing Theophrastus Because if ἀκανθίς occurs in Theophrastus or in an ancient gloss on Theophrastus, that could be the missing bridge between the bird-name and the botanical ἄκανθα. And there's a particularly good reason to do it: Theophrastus is chronologically prior to both the PGM and the later magical tradition. If akanthis appears here as a botanical or bird term, we would have an early source for exactly the lexical ambiguity that later appears in PGM XII. So my current verdict after checking him is: No Acanthian dove yet. But Theophrastus gives us an important ancient source for the ἀκανθ-/ἄκανθα vocabulary, including exotic, resinous, poisonous “thorn” plants. The next step is to check whether the actual form ἀκανθίς occurs anywhere in Theophrastus or in the ancient/Byzantine transmission of his botanical terminology. That is a much more promising search than simply searching the phrase “Acanthian Dove.” [QUERENT] [not in the paste] [ANSWER 7] I checked the Nag Hammadi corpus specifically, including searches for the relevant Greek/Coptic vocabulary and the major tractates. The result is useful, but unfortunately it is not yet the ancient “Acanthian Dove” witness we're hoping for. What I find The Nag Hammadi codices themselves are Coptic translations of works that were generally composed in Greek, so this is exactly the sort of corpus where a Greek term can disappear into a Coptic equivalent and become difficult to recognize by English keyword searching. The authoritative Coptic Gnostic Library Online provides the Coptic texts, translations, introductions, and indexes. I searched particularly for the equivalents of: ἀκανθίς / ἀκανθίδος ἄκανθος / ἄκανθα Ἀκάνθιος itself searches the collection's texts and phrases, and the full corpus consists of the 52 tractates preserved in the codices. /Greek mythological material, archontic beings, astronomical powers, primordial humanity, and revelatory material. It as the daughter of Autonous and Hippodamia; after the death of her brother Anthus, the absent from one version, we can sometimes recover the underlying Greek tradition by comparing the parallel Coptic Ἀκανθίς / Ἀκανθυλλίς περιστερά — dove/pigeon πελειά / πελειάς — dove τρυγών — turtle-dove thorn/thistle + bird dove + messenger/angel dove + revelation dove + light/Spirit I do not find a Nag Hammadi passage that can responsibly be translated as “Acanthian Dove.” The online Nag Hammadi search facility itself searches the collection's texts and phrases, and the full corpus consists of the 52 tractates preserved in the codices. But there is one important qualification “No hit” is much less conclusive here than it would be for a Greek papyrus. The manuscripts are written in Coptic, and the underlying Greek originals are mostly lost. The collection therefore could preserve a Greek conceptual or lexical tradition without preserving the Greek word ἀκανθίς itself. And that makes the Greek originals of Nag Hammadi tractates particularly interesting for our investigation. The tractates I'd put at the top of the list I don't think we should treat all 52 texts equally. Several are much more likely to preserve the sort of material you're remembering. 1. On the Origin of the World This is probably my #1 Nag Hammadi target. It contains an extraordinarily syncretic cosmology involving Genesis, Egyptian/Greek mythological material, archontic beings, astronomical powers, primordial humanity, and revelatory material. It exists in two Nag Hammadi copies, which is useful because we can compare the Coptic witnesses. If “Acanthian” turns out to be a corrupted memory of a plant, bird, epithet, or mythological name, this is precisely the sort of tractate where I'd expect the underlying tradition to occur. 2. The Hypostasis of the Archons Also extremely promising because it contains mythological reinterpretations of Genesis and material concerning Eve, the serpent, the rulers, Sophia, and heavenly beings. A bird/dove image could easily be involved in a secondary Greek tradition even if the surviving Coptic text doesn't preserve the exact word. 3. The Gospel of the Egyptians This is another major candidate. It is packed with ritual, sacred names, heavenly beings, Sethian cosmology, baptismal imagery, and secret revelation. The text actually calls itself the “Holy Book of the Great Invisible Spirit” and contains long sequences of sacred names and powers. That makes it much more promising for your memory than, say, Thomas. 4. The Three Steles of Seth Again, ritual/revelatory material rather than narrative prose. It contains sequences of divine names and praise that could easily generate a remembered epithet. 5. Trimorphic Protennoia Very high priority because of its elaborate language of voice, revelation, descent, light, and the divine feminine. If your remembered “dove” was actually functioning as a voice/messenger/revelatory entity, this kind of text is much more promising than a straightforward Gnostic narrative. 6. The Thunder: Perfect Mind Another text I'd keep in the search set because of its unusual first-person divine voice and its imagery of identity, manifestation, concealment, and revelation. But I found something potentially more important outside the exact word search The Nag Hammadi material contains Egyptian/Gnostic transformations of older Greek mythological material. For example, On the Origin of the World and the Hypostasis of the Archons preserve traditions in which biblical Genesis is reworked through a cosmological vocabulary that is demonstrably interacting with wider late-antique mythological traditions. So if the thing you remember was something like: “the Acanthian Dove” I would now seriously entertain the possibility that “Acanthian” was not a geographical adjective at all. It could be the English form of a Greek personal name: Ἀκανθίς And that matters enormously because Ἀκανθίς is independently a mythological woman who becomes a bird. The ancient mythographical tradition identifies Acanthis/Acanthyllis as the daughter of Autonous and Hippodamia; after the death of her brother Anthus, the family is transformed into birds. Acanthis becomes a bird associated with the thistle. So we have a genuine ancient entity: Acanthis → transformed into a bird rather than merely: “Acanthian = from Acanthus.” That is a very different possible origin for your memory. And now something I want to flag as genuinely tantalizing The Greek word ἀκανθίς has a complicated semantic history. The standard LSJ tradition gives it as a bird (goldfinch), citing Aristotle and Theocritus. But other lexical traditions give ἀκανθίς botanical meanings as well. And the magical PGM XII passage literally has: αἷμα ἀπ᾽ ὤμου — ἄκανθις “blood from the shoulder — akanthis.” That is the magical text we've already identified. So there are now three independent ancient trajectories around the same word: And that makes the Greek originals of Nag Hammadi tractates particularly interesting for our investigation. The tractates I'd put at the top of the list I don't think we should treat all 52 texts equally. Several are much more likely to preserve the sort of material you're remembering. 1. On the Origin of the World If “Acanthian” turns out to be a corrupted memory of a plant, bird, epithet, or mythological name, this is precisely the sort of tractate where I'd expect the underlying tradition to occur. 2. The Hypostasis of the Archons Also extremely promising because it contains mythological reinterpretations of Genesis and material concerning Eve, the serpent, the rulers, Sophia, and heavenly beings. 3. The Gospel of the Egyptians ἀκανθίς = bird Ἀκανθίς = mythological woman transformed into a bird ἄκανθις = a mysterious magical ingredient in PGM XII And then separately: dove = an important magical animal in the PGM dove = prophetic/sacred bird in Greek religious tradition That is a remarkably dense intersection. One thing I would not do I would not yet say: “Nag Hammadi confirms the Acanthian Dove.” It doesn't. And I don't want to let the pattern become self-confirming just because we're finding lots of interesting associations. Instead, I think we're now at the point where the right question is: Is there a Greek or Coptic magical/gnostic text in which Ἀκανθίς (or a Coptic equivalent of it) is associated with a dove, messenger, revelation, light, or divine voice? That's a much sharper question. The next corpus I would hit I'd actually move beyond Nag Hammadi now and search the related late-antique material in this order: Pistis Sophia Berlin Gnostic Codex 8502 Greek fragments underlying Nag Hammadi texts Askew Codex / Bruce Codex Greek magical papyri outside PGM Coptic magical papyri Christian magical papyri Greek magical handbooks and formularies The Kyranides Byzantine magical/medical lexica Hesychius and Photius Scholia on Aristotle/Theocritus Antoninus Liberalis + lost Ornithogonia material The reason I'm increasingly interested in Pistis Sophia and the Coptic magical material is that they sit much closer to the intersection we're looking for: Gnostic revelation + ritual + secret names + birds/animals + Greek magical vocabulary, whereas Nag Hammadi proper gives us relatively little evidence for the literal phrase. And importantly, the Nag Hammadi corpus has multiple textual witnesses to some works, so where a term looks absent from one version, we can sometimes recover the underlying Greek tradition by comparing the parallel Coptic copies. So: Nag Hammadi doesn't give us the Dove yet. But it hasn't killed the hypothesis. If anything, it pushes me toward the possibility that we're looking for a Greek term/name that got translated or transformed before reaching the surviving Coptic manuscripts. The next place I'd go is Pistis Sophia + the Askew/Bruce/Greek-Gnostic material, while simultaneously checking the actual Greek fragments of the Nag Hammadi works. That's where I think our chances of finding the missing “Acanthian” are better.
